title: Working in software outsourcing: scope, clients and shipping on contract
summary: In outsourcing you build someone else's product to an agreement. How scope, change requests, billing and time zones shape the job, and how to grow a career there.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
A client messages at 9 p.m. their time: "Small thing, can the export also include last year's invoices? Should be quick." It probably is quick, half a day at most. You say yes because you want to be helpful. Two weeks later there have been nine of these small things, the sprint is late, and the status meeting opens with "why did delivery slip?"

If you've worked in outsourcing, you've probably lived some version of that. People outside the industry picture a code factory. A good services firm is much more interesting: you build real products for real businesses, and you often see more domains in a couple of years than you would inside one product company. My first agency job, at Splus Software from 2019 to 2020, put me on 8+ client projects across education, F&B, banking and e-commerce, from requirements all the way to handover. It's also where I led a small team for the first time.

This post closes the series that started with big corp vs startup vs outsourcing, next to the deep dives on big corps and startups. Here we'll cover the one structural fact behind services work, the two shapes the work takes, scope and change requests, money, communication across time zones, quality, and how careers grow.

You build it, the client owns it

In a product company you build what your company sells. In services, a client pays your company to build what they sell. Most of what feels different follows from that one fact:

  • The client owns the what: requirements, priorities, the product vision. Your team owns the how, the delivery and the quality bar.
  • Your direct customer is the client. End users still matter a lot, but the person who signs off acceptance and renews the contract is the client.
  • Your hours are billed, so how you spend them is visible in a way product engineers rarely experience.
  • The relationship is an asset. Happy clients renew and refer you. Unhappy ones leave, however clean the code was.

One line from the Agile Manifesto fits services work well: "Customer collaboration over contract negotiation." The authors are careful to add that there is value in the items on the right, they just value the ones on the left more (Manifesto for Agile Software Development). In outsourcing you live with both every day. The contract sets the frame, and daily collaboration decides whether the project actually goes well.

Two things to ship

Every services project ships two things: the software, and what it felt like to work with your team. A technically solid project with poor communication still feels like a bad project to the client. Engineers who get this early tend to become the ones clients ask for by name.

The two shapes of outsourcing work

"Outsourcing" covers two very different day-to-day jobs, and which one you're in changes almost everything:

ModelWhat the day looks likeWho owns delivery
Staff augmentationYou join the client's team as an individual and work like one of their engineers, inside their process and toolsThe client's team. You contribute to it
Project / managed deliveryYour company takes on a whole project, and your team delivers it end to end against an agreed scopeYour services team, until handover

Staff augmentation feels closest to product work. You sit inside the client's team, follow their rituals, and the main relationship skill is being a great teammate in someone else's house. Managed delivery is where the services-specific muscles get the hardest workout: scope, estimates that turn into commitments, demos, acceptance, and the relationship at the account level. The rest of this post leans toward managed delivery, because that's where mistakes cost the most.

Scope protects both sides

In a product company, "let's just add this" is normal. In services, every "just add this" lands on top of an agreed scope. That boundary protects the client's budget and your team's evenings. The skill newcomers most often lack is handling a change out loud instead of absorbing it.

  • Scope creep rarely shows up as one big request. It's ten small ones, each reasonable on its own, and together they eat the whole buffer.
  • A change request shows the trade-off. "Happy to do that. It's outside what we agreed, so I'll write it up with the effort and the impact on the date, and you decide." You're handing the client a choice.
  • Confirm agreements in writing. "As discussed on the call: X is in this phase, Y moves to phase 2." One friendly message today saves an awkward argument three weeks from now.

Change requests have a dark side, and it helps to know it. Martin Fowler describes contracting companies that "deliberately low-bid the fixed price, with the explicit plan of making a profit on change requests" (FixedScopeMirage). A client who has been burned that way will read every CR with suspicion. So make yours boringly honest: small, explained, priced the same way every time, and raised the day you notice the change. Don't save them up for the invoice.

Saying yes to everything isn't kindness

Absorbing extra scope to dodge an awkward conversation feels generous. It also teaches the client that scope is free, wears your team down, and ends in a much worse conversation once the budget is gone. A clear boundary, said early and kindly, protects the relationship better.

Billing, estimates and utilization

Money is visible in services in a way it isn't elsewhere. Knowing the model makes a lot of daily pressure make sense:

ConceptWhat it meansWhy you should care
Time & materials (T&M)The client pays for the hours workedHonest time tracking matters, and scope can flex more easily
Fixed bidAn agreed price for an agreed scopeEstimates become commitments. Overruns come out of your company's margin, so scope discipline keeps the project alive
UtilizationThe share of your time that's billableThe core metric of a services business. It explains the pull toward client work over internal projects
BenchTime between client engagementsCosts the company money, and is often your best window for learning

The big consequence: on a fixed-bid project, your estimate is a promise your company has already sold. A careless one can wipe out the project's margin. That's why services firms care about estimation more than many startups do, and why the honest estimation habits from Agile and Scrum in practice count for even more here.

Fixed price doesn't have to mean everything is frozen, though. Fowler argues that a fixed-price contract can run in an agile way if you fix price and time and let scope move. His example plan starts with "we have $x to spend and we need a release on 1 Dec," and the feature list gets worked out together as the team learns (FixedPrice). Not every client will buy that, but it's a far better opening than pretending a 40-page spec has captured everything.

Communication is part of what you deliver

In a product team, too many updates can be noise. In services, your communication is the part of the project the client sees every day. The bar is higher and the form is more deliberate:

  • Status updates with no surprises. Bad news goes out early. A client who sees a slip coming two weeks out can plan around it. A client who hears about it on delivery day stops trusting every update after that.
  • Demos as proof. Working software on a regular cadence answers "are they actually making progress?" better than any report, and scope questions come up naturally while people click around.
  • Risks come with options. "We may miss the 15th because the payment sandbox is still down. Option A: ship without refunds and add them next sprint. Option B: move the date by a week."
  • Write things down: decisions, scope, acceptance criteria. When the relationship runs on an agreement, the written record is what everyone goes back to.

Time zones and distributed delivery

Outsourcing is often cross-border, so the time-zone gap is a constraint you deal with every single day. There's solid data on what distance costs. James Herbsleb and Audris Mockus studied change data from a telecom software organization at Lucent and found that work items spread across sites took about 2.5 times as long to complete as similar items done at one site. They repeated the analysis in a second organization and got the same main result. The mechanism they found was simple: distributed items pulled in more people, and the number of people involved was strongly related to how long an item took (An Empirical Study of Speed and Communication in Globally Distributed Software Development, IEEE TSE, 2003).

That gives you a few practical habits:

  • Write messages someone can answer without a meeting: full context, the exact question, and what you'll do if you don't hear back. A bare "got a sec?" across a seven-hour gap can cost a whole day.
  • Keep the number of people on each item small. If a ticket needs three people on two continents to agree, it will crawl. Give one person on each side the authority to decide.
  • Save the overlap window for things that really need real time: decisions, demos, unblocking.
  • Make the work visible async with tickets, written status and recorded demos, so nobody has to wonder what happened overnight.

Engineers who write clear, self-contained async messages are worth a lot in this world, and it's a skill you can practice on purpose. For the receiving end of that, see making handoffs easier to receive.

Quality under contract

In services, the contract and the client's expectations define quality. The hardest moments come from the gap between a fixed budget and a client who expects everything. A few habits help:

  • Make trade-offs explicit. "Within this budget we can do A and B well. C needs about two more weeks. Which matters most to you?" Let the client make that call early, while there's still room to change plans.
  • Hold a baseline you won't cross. Security, data integrity and anything that could hurt the client's users stay non-negotiable, even under deadline pressure.
  • Plan the handover from day one. Someone else will inherit this code. Docs, a clear structure and a knowledge-transfer plan are part of the deliverable, and they often decide whether you get a referral or a complaint.

Failure modes to watch for

Failure modeWhat it looks likeWhat helps
Silent scope creepAbsorbing "small" extras until you're over budget and somehow it's your faultName changes early, use change requests, confirm scope in writing
Order-taker modeBuilding exactly what's asked even when you can see it won't workSay what you see and suggest an alternative. Clients pay for judgment too
Hidden bad newsSitting on a slip until it blows up at the deadlineRaise risks early, with options
Shallow contextNever staying on a product long enough to learn how it really worksGo deep within each engagement, and favor firms with long-term clients
Burnout from the squeezeYour team working nights to cover the gap between budget and expectationsPut the trade-off in front of the client and keep a pace you can sustain

How to grow a career in services

Outsourcing rewards a particular mix of skills, and it offers a career shape the other worlds don't:

  • Be the advisor in the room. The engineers clients ask for by name understand the client's business, push back with reasons, and help the client look good to their own boss. That reputation travels with you.
  • Treat the relationship as a craft. Setting expectations, writing a clear update and raising a risk without drama are learnable skills, and they carry over to any senior role.
  • Use the variety. Several domains and stacks in a few years is a real gift. Collect that breadth on purpose, and go as deep as each engagement allows.
  • Pick a ladder. Services careers often split into a technical track (tech lead, architect, principal) and a client-facing track (delivery lead, engagement manager, account lead). Notice which kind of problem gives you energy.

If not owning a product long-term starts to bother you, treat that as useful information. It might pull you toward a startup or a big corp where you live with one product for years. None of these is a one-way door, and the scope, communication and delivery habits you build in services make you stronger wherever you go next.

Try this week

  • The next time a "small thing" lands, reply with a one-line scope check: in the current scope, or a change request?
  • Rewrite your next status update so the client could act on it without a call.
  • Pick one risk you've been sitting on and raise it today, with two options.
  • Look at your slowest open ticket and count the people who have to agree on it. See if you can drop one.
  • Write a one-page handover note for the module you know best, as if you were leaving next month.

faqs.q: Is working in outsourcing just being a code factory?
faqs.a: In a good services firm, no. You build real products for real businesses and usually see more domains and stacks than you would inside one product company. The real difference is ownership: the client owns the product and its direction, your team owns how it gets built and delivered, and managing the client relationship sits right next to the engineering.

faqs.q: How do I handle scope creep without upsetting the client?
faqs.a: Make the trade-off visible early. Say something like "Happy to do that. It's outside what we agreed, so I'll write it up with the effort and the impact on the date, and you decide." Confirm agreements in writing after calls. Keep change requests small, explained and priced consistently, so the client never feels they're being used to pad the invoice.

faqs.q: What is the difference between time and materials and a fixed-bid contract?
faqs.a: Under time and materials, the client pays for the hours worked, so scope can flex more easily. Under a fixed bid, the price is agreed for an agreed scope, so your estimate becomes a commitment and any overrun comes out of your company's margin. Martin Fowler argues fixed price can still work in an agile way if price and date are fixed and scope is allowed to move.

faqs.q: Why is communication so important in outsourcing?
faqs.a: Because the client experiences the project mostly through your communication. Status updates with no surprises, regular demos, risks raised early with options, and written decisions build trust. Across time zones it matters even more: in Herbsleb and Mockus's study, work spread across sites took about 2.5 times as long as similar work at one site, largely because more people got involved.

faqs.q: What does a career path look like in software services?
faqs.a: It often splits into a technical track (tech lead, architect, principal) and a client-facing track (delivery lead, engagement manager, account lead). On either track, the most valuable thing you build is a reputation as someone clients trust: you understand their business, push back with reasons and raise problems early.
